description: Nand: engineers from Tashkent. We're building a real-time game-engine fire simulation driven by NASA microgravity combustion data, with Dashboard and AI assistant that explains it.
summary:
Flamelet is an interactive website that shows what NASA actually knows about fire in the air astronauts breathe. You pick a cabin (ISS, EVA prep, Moon base, spacesuit or Apollo 1). Flamelet then relights every matching flame from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) microgravity-combustion data, ranks the investigations by how many tests fall inside that cabin's air, and opens each test at true scale.

For the "Flame in Freefall" challenge, it turns thousands of rows from six NASA investigations (FLEX, CFI, CFI-G, Flame Design, BASS-II and Saffire-II) into something you can see and compare. It also shows where the data stops. For air nobody has tested, a Fire-X lite flame model lets you explore a what-if, always labelled as a model.

Every number carries a badge: recorded by NASA, computed from NASA's values, model, or no data. Each test links back to its source file and line. A small guide, Flamey, explains anything you click.

It matters because cabin atmospheres are changing, and fire-safety decisions should rest on honest evidence, including knowing what hasn't been tested.
details:
Flamelet lets you ask what NASA actually knows about fire in the air people will breathe.

What it does: You pick a cabin (ISS, EVA prep, Moon base, spacesuit or Apollo 1) and the site relights every matching flame from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) microgravity-combustion repository. It ranks the investigations by how many tests fall inside that cabin's air, and it opens each test at true scale. Where nobody has run a test, you can explore a "what-if" with a flame model that is labelled as a model.

Honesty: Every number on screen carries a badge: plain means NASA recorded it, ƒ means computed from NASA's values, ≈ means model, and ∅ means no data. The tables are unchanged, and every test links back to its source file and line. This is meant for people who need to trust the numbers, including combustion scientists.

Flamey: A small flame guide explains any element when you click or right-click it. Its explanations are generated from the data rows. Optional follow-up questions are answered by Gemini from only the facts on screen, and we flag them as needing verification.

Built with: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no npm packages, so the site is static and opens from file://. Node scripts build the data and run 51 spec-number checks and 31 headless browser steps. The flame uses the Fire-X lite model (after Wrede et al., ACM TOG 2025). The follow-up endpoint is a Vercel serverless function. Claude, ChatGPT and Grok helped with code generation and debugging.

Creative angle: Instead of a data table, the flame itself is the interface, and the site says plainly where the data stops.NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository
dataRefs: PSI-159 ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases)
PSI-25 BASS-II (Burning and Suppression of Solids II)
projectRefs: Fire-X: Extinguishing Fire with Stoichiometric Heat Release (Wrede et al., ACM TOG 2025, CC BY 4.0), basis of the Fire-X lite flame model
Geist and Geist Mono font (SIL OFL)
